findings.issue_text: [BUG] The new denial cache short-circuits Check with no re-validation path: once a denial is cached, a subsequent permission grant is invisible until the TTL expires, whereas the positive cache was explicitly designed to self-heal by falling through to the database on a cached denial. A user who was denied access to a resource, then granted access (role change, dashboard permission added), keeps receiving Allowed=false for the full shortCacheTTL even though the database now allows them. The diff even adds the test 'Fallback to the database on outdated cache' proving the positive cache recovers on the very next request after a grant, but the symmetric recovery case for permDenialCache is neither implemented nor tested — no invalidation hook for the new cache is added anywhere in the diff, and any stale teamCache/basicRoleCache/folderCache data that produced the denial gets pinned for another TTL cycle.

[BUG] The permCache read was removed from getUserPermissions and getAnonymousPermissions but only reinstated on the Check and List paths via getCachedIdentityPermissions, so every other caller of getIdentityPermissions (e.g., the BatchCheck RPC that the AuthzServiceServer interface served before this change) now unconditionally performs the database query and then overwrites permCache without ever reading it. BatchCheck-style traffic that previously served most requests from permCache now hits the database on every call, a hot-path regression for the very workload (batched permission checks) this cache existed to protect, while still paying the cost of writing cache entries it never consumes.

[ADVISORY] TestService_CacheCheck never exercises the denial-cache write branch (service.go 'if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(...) }') — every case pre-seeds caches via direct Set calls, and no case performs a database-denied Check and asserts the denial entry was written, nor a case where a grant supersedes a cached denial. A regression in the write path (e.g., wrong key built, Set error swallowed, value type changed) or in stale-denial behavior ships green: the only denial-cache test verifies reads of a hand-planted entry, so the entire populate side of the new negative cache is uncovered by the tests added in this diff.

[BUG] userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates name and parent with single underscores, so distinct (name, parent) pairs collide: namespace + '.perm_' + userUID + '_' + action + '_' + name + '_' + parent produces the identical string for (name="a_b", parent="c") and (name="a", parent="b_c"). A denial legitimately cached for one resource (dashboard uid containing an underscore, or folder uid containing an underscore) is served as a denial for a different resource whose name/parent concatenate to the same key, incorrectly denying access to a dashboard the user can actually see, for the duration of the TTL. Resource UIDs in Grafana permit underscore characters, so this is reachable with real identifiers, not just crafted ones.

[ADVISORY] Every denied Check writes a permDenialCache entry keyed by attacker-influenced (name, parent) values with no size bound or rate limit on distinct entries created. A low-privilege or unauthenticated caller enumerating nonexistent dashboard/folder UIDs creates one local-cache entry per distinct denied name until TTL cleanup runs, so sustained probing inflates per-process memory on the authz service — a resource-exhaustion vector introduced by caching negatives on arbitrary, user-chosen keys.

[ADVISORY] getCachedIdentityPermissions duplicates the identity-type dispatch switch that already exists in getIdentityPermissions/getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions, creating a second hand-maintained enumeration that must be kept in sync — with drift already visible: the cached switch returns cache.ErrNotFound for types.TypeRenderService while the DB switch has full render-service handling. The next change to identity handling (new identity type, changed render-service semantics, altered actionSets resolution) gets applied to one switch and not the other; a drift in the cached switch silently serves wrong or missing cached permissions for Check/List while the DB fallback path behaves differently, and the divergence is invisible until a cache-hit-dependent test fails.

[BUG] When cached permissions are found but deny the check, the code falls through to the database and increments permissionCacheUsage with label "false", recording a cache hit as a cache miss. The permissionCacheUsage hit-rate metric that distinguishes "served from cache" from "went to the store" undercounts hits for every cached-deny-then-DB-recheck request, skewing the observability signal operators would use to evaluate this caching change and to tune shortCacheTTL after rollout.

[BUG] The new permission denial cache short-circuits Check before any database consultation and has no invalidation path anywhere in the diff, so a permission granted to a previously denied resource keeps returning Allowed:false until shortCacheTTL expiry. Sequence: a Check for (user, action, name, parent) is denied once and cached at line 153-155; an admin then grants the permission; every subsequent Check hits the denial entry at line 117 and returns deny without consulting the DB — even though the diff's own 'Fallback to the database on outdated cache' design (and test at service_test.go:947) exists precisely so grants are picked up immediately on the allow path. Grant latency is therefore ~0 for never-denied resources but up to shortCacheTTL for previously denied ones, an asymmetry the caching-improvement intent does not account for and that no Delete/invalidation hook in this diff mitigates.

[BUG] The only remaining permission-cache read sites are getCachedIdentityPermissions and it hard-returns cache.ErrNotFound for TypeRenderService, while the generic cache read this diff deletes from getUserPermissions (old lines around new 379-380) previously served that identity type — so render-service permission checks no longer read from cache at all. Every render-service Check/List now goes through the full store path (getUserPermissions → singleflight → permissionStore.GetUserPermissions) on each request, a regression for rendering traffic that the PR title 'improve authz caching' contradicts. If the removal of the in-function cache read was intended to centralize reads in getCachedIdentityPermissions, the render-service case was left un-migrated.

[ADVISORY] The embedded client's 30-second local cache is silently replaced with NoopCache while newRemoteRBACClient (line ~160) keeps its 30-second cache, giving the same logical service different staleness and double-caching characteristics depending on deployment mode. Remote-server deployments now stack client-side 30s staleness on top of the new server-side permCache and permDenialCache TTLs, so revocations and denials propagate faster on embedded instances than on remote ones — operators tuning TTLs see inconsistent behavior with nothing in the diff explaining or flagging the divergence; also the embedded path regressed from a cached client to an uncached one, adding a gRPC hop cost per Check for cases the Service cache does not cover.

[ADVISORY] getCachedIdentityPermissions duplicates getIdentityPermissions' identity-type switch (anonymous / render service / user+service-account / default-error) as a second hand-maintained dispatch table that must be updated in lockstep. When a new identity type is added or an existing case changes, updating one switch and not the other silently bypasses the cache (falling back to the store path, degrading the very metric this PR optimizes) or produces divergent error behavior — getCachedIdentityPermissions' default returns 'unsupported identity type' which Check/List swallow (err == nil / else-branch) before re-hitting the same error in getIdentityPermissions, so the two paths report different errors for the same input.

[ADVISORY] On every permCache miss, Check resolves the identity twice: getCachedIdentityPermissions calls s.GetUserIdentifiers, then the fallback path calls getIdentityPermissions → getUserPermissions which resolves it again. For each cache-miss Check where the idCache is also cold (first request after TTL expiry), the store now serves two identity lookups where one sufficed before this diff — a hot-path regression on exactly the miss traffic the singleflight group was protecting.

[ADVISORY] The permissionCacheUsage metric no longer measures what it did: denial-cache hits increment 'true' for the permission cache, and a genuine permCache hit whose checkPermission returns false falls through and increments 'false'. Dashboards and alerts built on permissionCacheUsage now undercount hits (cache-hit-but-denied requests are recorded as misses) and conflate two distinct caches with different keys and semantics into one counter, so the effectiveness of this PR's own caching change cannot be correctly evaluated in production.

[ADVISORY] The denial cache creates one entry per (namespace, user, action, name, parent) tuple, raising cache cardinality from O(users×actions) to O(users×actions×resources). A user (or scripted client) enumerating dashboards it cannot access inserts a new cache entry per denied resource for the TTL window on every instance's local cache — memory growth proportional to denied-request cardinality that the previous per-(user,action) permission cache key did not have, with no size bound added in this diff.

[ADVISORY] The new tests cover only cache-hit allow, cache-miss allow, and an explicit denial hit; they never exercise the grant-after-deny sequence, the anonymous identity cached path in Check, or the unsupported-identity-type path through the new early-return logic. The stale-deny failure mode (denial entry short-circuiting the DB fallback after a permission grant) and the anonymous Check path added in getCachedIdentityPermissions would pass a regression unnoticed; a future change to the denial-check ordering or key construction at service.go:116-121 ships without any test signal.

[BUG] The new permDenialCache is written on every denied Check but has no invalidation path anywhere in the codebase — permission/role/team changes invalidate userPermCacheKey entries only, never userPermDenialCacheKey entries, so denial is TTL-only while the existing permission cache follows invalidate-on-change semantics. When an admin grants a user access to a resource (role change, team add, direct permission), the previously-denied Check result stays pinned in permDenialCache for shortCacheTTL and keeps returning Allowed=false even after permCache has been correctly invalidated and refetched — the user is denied access the UI says they have, and this PR silently changed the accepted propagation guarantee (grant-visible-on-invalidation) into TTL-bounded staleness without an explicit decision.

[BUG] The 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' test seeds userPermDenialCacheKey with parent "fold1" and sets request Folder: "fold1", but Check builds the denial key from checkReq.ParentFolder, so the seeded entry can never be read and the test passes via the cached-perms-deny → DB-fallback path instead of the denial-cache path it names. The only test named after the denial-cache read path exercises nothing of it — a regression that breaks denial-cache reads (e.g., a key-format change or a broken Get) would not fail this test, giving false coverage on the security-relevant negative-caching path.

[ADVISORY] Every denied Check inserts a fresh permDenialCache entry keyed by namespace+user+action+name+parent with no cardinality bound, no eviction beyond shortCacheTTL, and no write-side deduplication, so the cache key space grows with every distinct denied (user, resource) pair. Anonymous or low-privilege traffic enumerating resource UIDs (e.g., scraping dashboard UIDs that all deny) floods the local/remote cache with short-lived denial entries, evicting useful permCache/teamCache entries and raising memory pressure on shared cache backends — the operators of high-traffic instances get hit first, and nothing in this diff exposes or limits the growth.

[ADVISORY] getCachedIdentityPermissions duplicates the identity-type switch from getIdentityPermissions (anonymous/render/user/service-account/default) as a second hand-maintained dispatch over the same enum. The next identity type added to getIdentityPermissions but not to this switch silently gets zero permission caching (always ErrNotFound → full DB fetch) instead of a compile-time or test failure — the two dispatches will drift because nothing ties them together; a shared resolve-then-key helper would make the second switch unnecessary.

[ADVISORY] No test in this diff covers the permDenialCache write path — no case asserts that a Check denied by the database populates the denial cache, nor that a subsequent identical Check short-circuits on it, nor what happens when a denial entry coexists with a later grant. Combined with the seeded-key mismatch in the existing denial test, the write path and the TTL-staleness-on-grant behavior (the riskiest new semantics in this PR) have zero test coverage; a regression in the Set call or its TTL would ship undetected.

[BUG] userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates unescaped variable-length name and parent fields, so distinct (name, parent) pairs produce identical denial-cache keys. A denial cached for (name="a", parent="b_f1") and one for (name="a_b", parent="f1") both serialize to "org-1.perm_<uid>_dashboards:read_a_b_f1"; a check for one resource pair is answered with the cached denial of the other, so a user with access to dashboard a_b in folder f1 is denied because dashboard a in folder b_f1 was once denied (and vice versa). Grafana UIDs permit underscores, so the colliding values are reachable from real identifiers; the error is fail-closed (wrong deny, not wrong allow), but it produces intermittent, unreproducible authorization failures for the TTL of the entry.

[BUG] permDenialCache entries are written but never deleted anywhere in the diff, and the denial-cache check runs before the fresh-permission path, so a cached denial outlives the permission grant that should have reversed it. User is denied on a resource (denial cached via Set at service.go:154); an admin then grants the permission and the existing permCache invalidation fires. The next Check hits the permDenialCache branch at service.go:116-119 and returns Allowed:false immediately, never reaching getIdentityPermissions, so the grant is ineffective for the full shortCacheTTL even though the permission cache itself was correctly invalidated. The diff's own 'outdated cache' test shows allows are supposed to fall back to the database when the cache is stale; denials have no such fallback and no invalidation path.

[BUG] Denial-cache keys are built from unvalidated, attacker-influenced Name and ParentFolder strings with no cardinality bound, and the underlying local cache has no size limit, so denied checks create unbounded cache entries. Any authenticated user can issue Check requests with arbitrary Name/Folder values (the internal caller echoes resource identifiers from request paths); every denied response writes a new permDenialCache entry keyed by that raw string. Distinct random UIDs produce distinct keys that live for shortCacheTTL, so sustained probing grows the shared local cache without bound — a memory-pressure denial of service on the authz service reachable by ordinary API traffic. The pre-existing permCache key was bounded (action is from a fixed set, UID is server-resolved); this diff is the first place raw request strings become cache keys.

[ADVISORY] userPermDenialCacheKey omits identity type and uses raw checkReq.UserUID, while the allow path (getCachedIdentityPermissions) caches under the resolved store.UserIdentifiers.UID — the two caches use divergent identity key spaces for the same decision. Denial entries are shared across identity types whose UserUID strings collide: identities that carry an empty UserUID (anonymous, and render-service checks) all land in the same key space for a given namespace/action/name/parent, so a denial incurred by one identity denies the other until TTL. The mismatch also means any future change to how GetUserIdentifiers resolves or normalizes UIDs silently decouples the denial cache from the allow cache, and the next maintainer adding an invalidation or a new identity type must remember to update two different key derivations for one logical concept.

[ADVISORY] permissionCacheUsage telemetry no longer measures permission-cache usage: denial-cache hits are counted as hits of the permission cache, and permission-cache hits whose evaluation denies are counted as misses before falling through to the database. On a permDenialCache hit (line 117-120) the metric increments with label "true" even though permCache was never consulted; on a permCache hit where checkPermission denies (line 133), it increments "false" and the request pays a full DB read even though the cache was hit. Operators tuning shortCacheTTL or evaluating this feature's hit rate from the permissionCacheUsage series will read a number that mixes three distinct behaviors (denial-cache short-circuit, permission-cache allow, permission-cache miss/deny), making the cache appear more effective than it is and hiding the DB-load cost of the deny fall-through path.

[BUG] The "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" subtest cannot fail if the permDenialCache short-circuit in Check is deleted, because its cached-permission fixture is set to deny (map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}) even though its comment states the intent is to cache an ALLOW that the denial entry must override, and the request sets the Folder field while the lookup key is built from checkReq.ParentFolder so the pre-seeded denial key (with parent "fold1") likely never matches. The only test claiming to verify the new denial-cache short-circuit actually passes via the ordinary cached-deny fall-through-to-DB path (which also returns Allowed=false); a regression that removes or reorders the permDenialCache.Get check in service.go leaves this test green, giving false confidence that the feature this PR introduces is covered.

[ADVISORY] No test in this diff drives the permDenialCache.Set write path: every TestService_CacheCheck subtest pre-seeds the caches directly, and none runs a Check that produces a DB-backed denial and then asserts the denial was cached and served on a follow-up Check. The denial-cache round-trip (deny in DB -> Set on line ~153 of service.go -> subsequent Check short-circuits) is never verified end-to-end; a regression that stops populating the cache (wrong key, Set error swallowed, condition inverted) leaves the denial-cache fast path permanently dead while every test in the diff still passes. Test files checked: pkg/services/authz/rbac/service_test.go (the only test file touched by this diff; no other spec references permDenialCache or userPermDenialCacheKey).

[ADVISORY] The new getCachedIdentityPermissions is only exercised for TypeUser by the new tests; its TypeRenderService branch (hard-coded ErrNotFound forcing a store hit on every render check), its TypeAnonymous permCache read, and its default unsupported-identity-type error return have no test coverage introduced in this diff. The deliberate render-service always-miss decision and the anonymous cache-read relocation out of getAnonymousPermissions are behavior changes nobody pins, so a future edit that silently changes them (e.g., caching render-service perms, or dropping the anonymous branch) ships without a failing test; additionally the default-branch error is unobservable through Check/List because both callers swallow any getCachedIdentityPermissions error into the DB fallback, making that branch dead code as wired. Test files checked: pkg/services/authz/rbac/service_test.go only; no test in the diff references TypeAnonymous, TypeRenderService, or getCachedIdentityPermissions error paths.

[ADVISORY] The "List based on cached permissions" subtest relies on s.store being nil (so a cache-miss fallback would panic) to prove the cache path was taken, instead of asserting store non-invocation or the permissionCacheUsage metric. The test's cache-path guarantee is incidental: if setupService later gains a default fake store (or the fallback stops dereferencing it), the subtest keeps passing while actually exercising the DB path, silently losing its reason to exist; there is also no cache-miss subtest for the new List caching branch in this diff.

[BUG] The new permDenialCache entries written on every denied Check are never invalidated by any code path in the permission-change invalidation flow, unlike permCache entries which existing permission-update invalidation clears via userPermCacheKey-shaped keys. When an operator grants a user access to a resource (role change, dashboard share, team membership change), the invalidation that previously made the grant take effect immediately clears permCache but leaves the denial entry at 'namespace.perm_<uid>_<action>_<name>_<parent>' in place for the full shortCacheTTL — and the denial check at service.go:118-121 runs FIRST and explicitly overrides a cached Allow (the test 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' proves denial wins over an allow entry). The user continues to be denied access they now have, and the stale denial survives exactly the invalidation mechanism that made the pre-existing shortCacheTTL staleness acceptable.

[ADVISORY] The PR's stated goal is moving caching from the client into the service, but newRemoteRBACClient still wraps the client in cache.NewLocalCache (30s expiry), so remote-authz-server deployments now stack a 30s client-side cache on top of the new service-level permCache/permDenialCache, while the in-process path (rbac.go:101-104) was switched to NoopCache. On remote deployments a permission change is now delayed by shortCacheTTL plus the 30s client cache (the inner service cache invalidates, then the outer client LocalCache keeps serving the stale Check response), and revocations — the security-sensitive direction — are affected; meanwhile the same code path behaves differently in-process vs remote, so cache-invalidation bugs will be untestable against the remote configuration.

[ADVISORY] getCachedIdentityPermissions calls s.GetUserIdentifiers on every Check/List before probing permCache, and on a cache miss the subsequent getIdentityPermissions → getUserPermissions path calls GetUserIdentifiers again, doubling the identifier resolution per missed request. Every cache-missed Check (the common case for cold caches and for all denied checks, which always fall through to the full path per the 'outdated cache' flow) performs two identifier lookups instead of one, adding a redundant store/DB round trip on the hottest authz path; the change also silently increases load on idCache since the miss-side lookup runs even when the caller will discard the result on a permCache miss.

[BUG] permDenialCache entries are never deleted anywhere in this diff, and their key format (userPermDenialCacheKey) differs from userPermCacheKey, so any existing permission-change invalidation that targets the existing cache keys cannot clear them — while the denial-cache hit at the top of Check short-circuits before the DB fallback that was explicitly built to recover from stale denials. When an admin grants a user access to a resource (or changes their role/team membership, which invalidates permCache/idCache), a previously cached denial for that (user, action, name, folder) tuple keeps short-circuiting Check with Allowed=false until shortCacheTTL expires — the fall-through-to-DB-on-stale-deny behavior the diff itself adds tests for ('Fallback to the database on outdated cache') is defeated the first time a denial is cached, so permission grants stop taking effect on invalidation and only after TTL. The new test 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' also confirms denials override even a fresh cached allow, since the denial cache is consulted before permCache.

[ADVISORY] The shared newRBACClient helper was deleted rather than parameterized by cache option, leaving two independent authzlib.NewClient construction sites (in-process with &NoopCache{} here, remote with cache.NewLocalCache at lines ~160-166) that must be kept in sync by hand. The next tracer/client option added to one construction site silently diverges the other — e.g., a tracing or dial option added only to the remote client leaves the in-process client (which serves every check when Zanzana shadow mode is off) without it, and nothing in the code flags the drift.

goldens.comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the new `permDenialCache` is checked first and, on a hit, returns `Allowed: false` immediately (`if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { ... return &authzv1.CheckResponse{Allowed: false}, nil }`). Unlike the positive permission cache path (`getCachedIdentityPermissions` + `checkPermission`), which explicitly falls through to `getIdentityPermissions` when the cached permissions do not allow the request, there is no fallthrough/revalidation when a denial cache entry exists. The cache entry is set whenever the DB-backed check returns `!allowed` (`s.permDenialCache.Set(..., true)`), and the diff shows no invalidation hook for it. This introduces a verifiable behavior where a previously denied resource can remain denied until `shortCacheTTL` expires even if the underlying permissions have been granted in the DB in the meantime.

adjudication.rationale: The diff clearly removes permCache read-paths from both getUserPermissions (deleted the `s.permCache.Get` short-circuit) and getAnonymousPermissions (deleted the `s.permCache.Get` short-circuit). A new cache read helper getCachedIdentityPermissions is introduced, but it is only used by the Check and List RPC handlers (service.go: Check and List now call getCachedIdentityPermissions before falling back to getIdentityPermissions). Any other code path that calls getIdentityPermissions (or getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions indirectly) will no longer read from permCache and will always execute the store query (while likely still writing to cache inside those functions). This is a concrete performance/architecture regression risk grounded in the diff; however, the specific mention of BatchCheck as an existing caller is not verifiable from the provided diff alone, so this is not a provable functional bug from the diff snippet.

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check` a new negative-cache write path was added: after DB permission evaluation, `if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true) }` (service.go). The added tests in `TestService_CacheCheck` only (a) return Allowed=true from cached perms, (b) fall back to DB for Allowed=true, or (c) verify denial-cache *reads* using a manually pre-seeded `permDenialCache.Set(...)`. No test performs a DB-denied check and then asserts the denial entry was written (or that the generated key matches), so the populate side of the new denial cache is untested. This is a concrete, diff-grounded test coverage gap, not a proven runtime defect. The note about “grant supersedes a cached denial” isn’t behavior implemented in the diff (cached denial always short-circuits), but the core point about the write branch being unexercised is correct.

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the diff adds `permDenialCache` and unconditionally writes a denial entry on any `!allowed` result: `s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)` (service.go). The key is constructed from request-controlled fields: `userPermDenialCacheKey(..., checkReq.Action, checkReq.Name, checkReq.ParentFolder)` (service.go + cache.go). There is no bound/eviction policy shown for distinct keys (the cache in tests is `cache.NewLocalCache` configured only with TTL/cleanup, and nothing in this diff adds a max size or rate limiting). Therefore a caller who can issue many denied checks with varying `Name`/`Folder` can force creation of many distinct cache entries until TTL cleanup, increasing per-process memory usage—i.e., a resource-exhaustion risk introduced by this negative caching.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getCachedIdentityPermissions duplicates the identity-type dispatch switch that already exists in getIdentityPermissions/getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions, creating a second hand-maintained enumeration that must be kept in sync — with drift already visible: the cached switch returns cache.ErrNotFound for types.TypeRenderService while the DB switch has full render-service handling. The next change to identity handling (new identity type, changed render-service semantics, altered actionSets resolution) gets applied to one switch and not the other; a drift in the cached switch silently serves wrong or missing cached permissions for Check/List while the DB fallback path behaves differently, and the divergence is invisible until a cache-hit-dependent test fails.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `getCachedIdentityPermissions(...)` with its own `switch idType` (Anonymous/RenderService/User+ServiceAccount/default). That dispatch logic duplicates the identity-type branching already spread across the existing permission retrieval paths (`getIdentityPermissions`, `getUserPermissions`, `getAnonymousPermissions`). This creates a second hand-maintained enumeration that can drift. The diff itself shows an example of divergence: `getCachedIdentityPermissions` hard-codes `types.TypeRenderService` to `return nil, cache.ErrNotFound`, meaning the cache path will *never* use cached permissions for render-service identities and will always fall back to DB behavior, which may differ from how other identity types are cached/handled. This is a maintainability/architecture risk rather than a directly verifiable correctness bug in the diff (it still falls back to DB).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] When cached permissions are found but deny the check, the code falls through to the database and increments permissionCacheUsage with label "false", recording a cache hit as a cache miss. The permissionCacheUsage hit-rate metric that distinguishes "served from cache" from "went to the store" undercounts hits for every cached-deny-then-DB-recheck request, skewing the observability signal operators would use to evaluate this caching change and to tune shortCacheTTL after rollout.

adjudication.rationale: In Service.Check, after getCachedIdentityPermissions returns cachedPerms with err == nil, the code only increments permissionCacheUsage with label "true" when allowed == true and returns. If cachedPerms are found but checkPermission returns allowed == false, it falls through and then unconditionally executes s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", checkReq.Action).Inc(), thereby recording a cache hit as a miss for this cached-deny path (see the new block starting at permDenialKey and the subsequent unconditional metric increment before getIdentityPermissions).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The new permission denial cache short-circuits Check before any database consultation and has no invalidation path anywhere in the diff, so a permission granted to a previously denied resource keeps returning Allowed:false until shortCacheTTL expiry. Sequence: a Check for (user, action, name, parent) is denied once and cached at line 153-155; an admin then grants the permission; every subsequent Check hits the denial entry at line 117 and returns deny without consulting the DB — even though the diff's own 'Fallback to the database on outdated cache' design (and test at service_test.go:947) exists precisely so grants are picked up immediately on the allow path. Grant latency is therefore ~0 for never-denied resources but up to shortCacheTTL for previously denied ones, an asymmetry the caching-improvement intent does not account for and that no Delete/invalidation hook in this diff mitigates.

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the new `permDenialCache` is consulted first and immediately returns `Allowed:false` if the key exists (service.go around the added block using `userPermDenialCacheKey(...)` and `s.permDenialCache.Get(...)`). Later in the same method, when the DB-backed check determines `!allowed`, it writes that denial into `permDenialCache` (`s.permDenialCache.Set(...)`). The diff shows no corresponding `Delete`/invalidation hook for this denial cache, so if permissions are granted after a denial is cached, subsequent checks for the same (namespace,user,action,name,parent) will continue to be denied until the cache entry expires (shortCacheTTL). This also bypasses the newly added “fallback to DB on cache miss/outdated cache” behavior because the denial cache prevents reaching the DB path at all.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The only remaining permission-cache read sites are getCachedIdentityPermissions and it hard-returns cache.ErrNotFound for TypeRenderService, while the generic cache read this diff deletes from getUserPermissions (old lines around new 379-380) previously served that identity type — so render-service permission checks no longer read from cache at all. Every render-service Check/List now goes through the full store path (getUserPermissions → singleflight → permissionStore.GetUserPermissions) on each request, a regression for rendering traffic that the PR title 'improve authz caching' contradicts. If the removal of the in-function cache read was intended to centralize reads in getCachedIdentityPermissions, the render-service case was left un-migrated.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does centralize permission-cache reads into `getCachedIdentityPermissions()` (cache reads removed from `getUserPermissions()` and `getAnonymousPermissions()`), and that function explicitly returns `cache.ErrNotFound` for `types.TypeRenderService`. Since `Check()`/`List()` now only attempt a permission-cache read via `getCachedIdentityPermissions()` before falling back to `getIdentityPermissions()`, render-service requests will always bypass the permission cache and hit the store path. This is a concrete, diff-grounded performance/behavior change, but it’s not a correctness defect on its own (could be intentional), so it’s best classified as an important non-bug review issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The embedded client's 30-second local cache is silently replaced with NoopCache while newRemoteRBACClient (line ~160) keeps its 30-second cache, giving the same logical service different staleness and double-caching characteristics depending on deployment mode. Remote-server deployments now stack client-side 30s staleness on top of the new server-side permCache and permDenialCache TTLs, so revocations and denials propagate faster on embedded instances than on remote ones — operators tuning TTLs see inconsistent behavior with nothing in the diff explaining or flagging the divergence; also the embedded path regressed from a cached client to an uncached one, adding a gRPC hop cost per Check for cases the Service cache does not cover.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows the embedded/"in-process" client is now constructed with `authzlib.WithCacheClientOption(&NoopCache{})` in `ProvideAuthZClient`, disabling the authzlib client cache, while `newRemoteRBACClient` still builds an authzlib client with `cache.NewLocalCache` (30s expiry). At the same time, the server adds its own `permCache` and `permDenialCache` with TTLs. This creates deployment-dependent caching/staleness and, for remote mode, an extra client-side cache layer on top of server caches (potentially extending revocation/deny propagation vs embedded). It’s a real, diff-grounded behavioral/operational inconsistency and potential performance regression in embedded mode, but not an unequivocal defect solely from the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getCachedIdentityPermissions duplicates getIdentityPermissions' identity-type switch (anonymous / render service / user+service-account / default-error) as a second hand-maintained dispatch table that must be updated in lockstep. When a new identity type is added or an existing case changes, updating one switch and not the other silently bypasses the cache (falling back to the store path, degrading the very metric this PR optimizes) or produces divergent error behavior — getCachedIdentityPermissions' default returns 'unsupported identity type' which Check/List swallow (err == nil / else-branch) before re-hitting the same error in getIdentityPermissions, so the two paths report different errors for the same input.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `getCachedIdentityPermissions` with its own identity-type `switch` (anonymous / render service / user+service-account / default error). `Check` and `List` call it first and, on any non-nil error, simply fall back to `getIdentityPermissions` (e.g., `if err == nil { ... }` else fetch from store), so any mismatch between the two dispatch tables would bypass caching without failing the request. The duplication/lockstep-maintenance risk is directly visible, but the diff does not prove a current functional inconsistency with `getIdentityPermissions` (not shown), so this is a real maintainability/architecture concern rather than a verifiable bug introduced here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] On every permCache miss, Check resolves the identity twice: getCachedIdentityPermissions calls s.GetUserIdentifiers, then the fallback path calls getIdentityPermissions → getUserPermissions which resolves it again. For each cache-miss Check where the idCache is also cold (first request after TTL expiry), the store now serves two identity lookups where one sufficed before this diff — a hot-path regression on exactly the miss traffic the singleflight group was protecting.

adjudication.rationale: In the new Check flow, on a permCache miss it calls s.getCachedIdentityPermissions(...), which for user/service-account identities calls s.GetUserIdentifiers(ctx, ns, userID) before checking permCache. When that returns cache.ErrNotFound, Check falls back to s.getIdentityPermissions(...) which (for user/service-account) goes through getUserPermissions(...), and that function also calls s.GetUserIdentifiers(ctx, ns, userID) before proceeding. This makes identifier resolution happen twice per miss in the Check hot path. Whether that results in two *store* lookups depends on GetUserIdentifiers’ internal caching behavior (not shown), but the duplicated call chain is directly verifiable from the diff and is a plausible performance regression.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The permissionCacheUsage metric no longer measures what it did: denial-cache hits increment 'true' for the permission cache, and a genuine permCache hit whose checkPermission returns false falls through and increments 'false'. Dashboards and alerts built on permissionCacheUsage now undercount hits (cache-hit-but-denied requests are recorded as misses) and conflate two distinct caches with different keys and semantics into one counter, so the effectiveness of this PR's own caching change cannot be correctly evaluated in production.

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, a denial-cache hit (`permDenialCache.Get`) increments `permissionCacheUsage` with label `"true"` even though it is not a `permCache` hit, conflating two different caches/semantics into one metric (`permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("true", checkReq.Action).Inc()`). Also, when `getCachedIdentityPermissions` returns cached perms but `checkPermission` determines `allowed == false`, the code does not record a hit and falls through to `s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", checkReq.Action).Inc()`, meaning a real `permCache` hit that results in denial is counted as a miss. This is observable from the added control flow and metric increments in the diff; it affects metric meaning rather than request correctness.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The denial cache creates one entry per (namespace, user, action, name, parent) tuple, raising cache cardinality from O(users×actions) to O(users×actions×resources). A user (or scripted client) enumerating dashboards it cannot access inserts a new cache entry per denied resource for the TTL window on every instance's local cache — memory growth proportional to denied-request cardinality that the previous per-(user,action) permission cache key did not have, with no size bound added in this diff.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new per-denial cache: `permDenialCache *cacheWrap[bool]` keyed by `userPermDenialCacheKey(namespace, userUID, action, name, parent)` (see `cache.go`) and used in `Service.Check` to short-circuit denies and to `Set` an entry when `!allowed` (see `service.go`). This is a clear increase in cache key cardinality from the existing `permCache` keyed by `(namespace,user,action)` to `(namespace,user,action,name,parentFolder)`. The cache implementation shown/used in tests is a local in-memory cache (`cache.NewLocalCache(...)`) with TTL but no size bound added in this diff, so repeated denied requests over many resource names can grow memory usage proportionally during the TTL window. This is a concrete performance/DoS risk introduced by the change, not a functional correctness bug proven by the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new tests cover only cache-hit allow, cache-miss allow, and an explicit denial hit; they never exercise the grant-after-deny sequence, the anonymous identity cached path in Check, or the unsupported-identity-type path through the new early-return logic. The stale-deny failure mode (denial entry short-circuiting the DB fallback after a permission grant) and the anonymous Check path added in getCachedIdentityPermissions would pass a regression unnoticed; a future change to the denial-check ordering or key construction at service.go:116-121 ships without any test signal.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new early-return caching logic in `Service.Check` (permDenialCache short-circuit at `service.go` ~113-121) and a new cached-permissions path for `TypeAnonymous` (in `getCachedIdentityPermissions`, `service.go` ~339-372). The added tests (`TestService_CacheCheck`, `TestService_CacheList`) cover user cache-hit allow, cache-miss fallback allow, outdated cache fallback allow, and explicit denial cache-hit, but do not exercise (a) the anonymous identity cached branch, (b) the default/unsupported identity type error path in `getCachedIdentityPermissions`, or (c) a “grant-after-deny” scenario where a stale `permDenialCache` entry could continue to deny due to the new short-circuit ordering. These are specific, diff-grounded coverage gaps for newly introduced control flow rather than a proven runtime defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The new permDenialCache is written on every denied Check but has no invalidation path anywhere in the codebase — permission/role/team changes invalidate userPermCacheKey entries only, never userPermDenialCacheKey entries, so denial is TTL-only while the existing permission cache follows invalidate-on-change semantics. When an admin grants a user access to a resource (role change, team add, direct permission), the previously-denied Check result stays pinned in permDenialCache for shortCacheTTL and keeps returning Allowed=false even after permCache has been correctly invalidated and refetched — the user is denied access the UI says they have, and this PR silently changed the accepted propagation guarantee (grant-visible-on-invalidation) into TTL-bounded staleness without an explicit decision.

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the new `permDenialCache` is consulted first (`if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { return Allowed:false }`) and is populated on every denied check (`if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(..., true) }`). Within this diff there is no corresponding `Delete`/invalidation call for `permDenialCache` anywhere—only TTL via `shortCacheTTL`. This means a previously-denied decision can override fresh permission state (even if `permCache` or underlying permissions change) until the denial entry expires, causing incorrect authorization results after a grant.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' test seeds userPermDenialCacheKey with parent "fold1" and sets request Folder: "fold1", but Check builds the denial key from checkReq.ParentFolder, so the seeded entry can never be read and the test passes via the cached-perms-deny → DB-fallback path instead of the denial-cache path it names. The only test named after the denial-cache read path exercises nothing of it — a regression that breaks denial-cache reads (e.g., a key-format change or a broken Get) would not fail this test, giving false coverage on the security-relevant negative-caching path.

adjudication.rationale: The finding hinges on an asserted mismatch between the test setting `CheckRequest.Folder: "fold1"` and `Check` computing the denial cache key from `checkReq.ParentFolder`. In the diff we can see `Check` uses `checkReq.ParentFolder` when building `permDenialKey`, but we cannot see how `checkReq` is derived from the protobuf request (the mapping/conversion code is not shown). It is entirely plausible that `req.Folder` is mapped into `checkReq.ParentFolder`, in which case the seeded denial cache entry would be read and the test would exercise the denial-cache path as intended. Because the claimed mismatch (and the resulting “test passes via fallback path”) is not verifiable from the diff alone, the finding overstates what can be concluded.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Every denied Check inserts a fresh permDenialCache entry keyed by namespace+user+action+name+parent with no cardinality bound, no eviction beyond shortCacheTTL, and no write-side deduplication, so the cache key space grows with every distinct denied (user, resource) pair. Anonymous or low-privilege traffic enumerating resource UIDs (e.g., scraping dashboard UIDs that all deny) floods the local/remote cache with short-lived denial entries, evicting useful permCache/teamCache entries and raising memory pressure on shared cache backends — the operators of high-traffic instances get hit first, and nothing in this diff exposes or limits the growth.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `permDenialCache` and in `Service.Check` unconditionally writes `s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)` for every `!allowed` result, where `permDenialKey` is composed of namespace+userUID+action+name+parentFolder (`userPermDenialCacheKey(...)`). This creates one cache entry per distinct denied (user, action, resource name, parent) tuple with no bound in this code beyond whatever `shortCacheTTL` provides, and it shares the same cache backend as other caches (`permCache`, `teamCache`, etc.). While not a functional correctness defect, it is a diff-grounded performance/operational risk: high-cardinality denied checks can churn/pressure the cache and evict more valuable entries.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getCachedIdentityPermissions duplicates the identity-type switch from getIdentityPermissions (anonymous/render/user/service-account/default) as a second hand-maintained dispatch over the same enum. The next identity type added to getIdentityPermissions but not to this switch silently gets zero permission caching (always ErrNotFound → full DB fetch) instead of a compile-time or test failure — the two dispatches will drift because nothing ties them together; a shared resolve-then-key helper would make the second switch unnecessary.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `getCachedIdentityPermissions` with its own `switch idType` dispatch (anonymous → cache key, render service → ErrNotFound, user/service account → identifiers+cache key, default → error). This duplicates the identity-type branching that already exists in `getIdentityPermissions` (which is called immediately after a cache miss in `Check` and `List`). Because the two switches are separate and hand-maintained, adding a new `types.IdentityType` handled in `getIdentityPermissions` but not in `getCachedIdentityPermissions` would silently disable caching for that identity type (always `cache.ErrNotFound` and fall back to DB), matching the finding’s drift concern. This is a maintainability/architecture issue rather than a current correctness bug shown in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] No test in this diff covers the permDenialCache write path — no case asserts that a Check denied by the database populates the denial cache, nor that a subsequent identical Check short-circuits on it, nor what happens when a denial entry coexists with a later grant. Combined with the seeded-key mismatch in the existing denial test, the write path and the TTL-staleness-on-grant behavior (the riskiest new semantics in this PR) have zero test coverage; a regression in the Set call or its TTL would ship undetected.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new permDenialCache write path in Service.Check: after the DB-backed permission check, it does `if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true) }` and an early-return read path at the top of Check (`if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { return Allowed:false }`). The new tests only cover the read path by pre-seeding `s.permDenialCache.Set(...)` in `TestService_CacheCheck/"Should deny on explicit cache deny entry"`, but there is no test that (a) causes a DB denial and asserts the denial cache was populated, nor (b) repeats the same Check to assert the short-circuit happens due to the previously written denial entry, nor (c) exercises the new “deny persists until TTL even if later granted” semantics. This is a specific, diff-grounded missing-coverage issue for newly added behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates unescaped variable-length name and parent fields, so distinct (name, parent) pairs produce identical denial-cache keys. A denial cached for (name="a", parent="b_f1") and one for (name="a_b", parent="f1") both serialize to "org-1.perm_<uid>_dashboards:read_a_b_f1"; a check for one resource pair is answered with the cached denial of the other, so a user with access to dashboard a_b in folder f1 is denied because dashboard a in folder b_f1 was once denied (and vice versa). Grafana UIDs permit underscores, so the colliding values are reachable from real identifiers; the error is fail-closed (wrong deny, not wrong allow), but it produces intermittent, unreproducible authorization failures for the TTL of the entry.
matched_golden_ids: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate describes the same underlying issue: cache key construction via underscore-delimited string concatenation without escaping/length-prefixing, allowing ambiguous keys and collisions when components contain underscores. It even provides a concrete collision example and explains the resulting incorrect denial cache hits affecting permissions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] permDenialCache entries are written but never deleted anywhere in the diff, and the denial-cache check runs before the fresh-permission path, so a cached denial outlives the permission grant that should have reversed it. User is denied on a resource (denial cached via Set at service.go:154); an admin then grants the permission and the existing permCache invalidation fires. The next Check hits the permDenialCache branch at service.go:116-119 and returns Allowed:false immediately, never reaching getIdentityPermissions, so the grant is ineffective for the full shortCacheTTL even though the permission cache itself was correctly invalidated. The diff's own 'outdated cache' test shows allows are supposed to fall back to the database when the cache is stale; denials have no such fallback and no invalidation path.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new negative cache (permDenialCache) that is consulted first in Service.Check: if permDenialCache.Get(...) hits, the method immediately returns Allowed:false (service.go ~113-119) and never reaches either cached-permissions allow check or the fresh getIdentityPermissions DB path. The code also writes permDenialCache entries when a check is denied (service.go ~150-154), but the diff shows no corresponding Delete/invalidation anywhere for permDenialCache (only a TTL via newCacheWrap). As a result, if underlying permissions change during the TTL window, the cached denial will continue to override fresh state and prevent the “outdated cache falls back to DB” behavior that the new logic provides for permCache.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Denial-cache keys are built from unvalidated, attacker-influenced Name and ParentFolder strings with no cardinality bound, and the underlying local cache has no size limit, so denied checks create unbounded cache entries. Any authenticated user can issue Check requests with arbitrary Name/Folder values (the internal caller echoes resource identifiers from request paths); every denied response writes a new permDenialCache entry keyed by that raw string. Distinct random UIDs produce distinct keys that live for shortCacheTTL, so sustained probing grows the shared local cache without bound — a memory-pressure denial of service on the authz service reachable by ordinary API traffic. The pre-existing permCache key was bounded (action is from a fixed set, UID is server-resolved); this diff is the first place raw request strings become cache keys.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new denial cache key that incorporates raw request fields: `userPermDenialCacheKey(namespace, userUID, action, name, parent)` concatenates `checkReq.Name` and `checkReq.ParentFolder` (`service.go`), and on every denied check it unconditionally writes `s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)`. Unlike the existing `permCache` keys (based on server-resolved user UID + action), this new key space can grow with attacker-controlled `Name`/`Folder` values. The cache shown in this PR is a local in-memory cache configured only with TTL/cleanup (e.g., `cache.NewLocalCache(cache.Config{Expiry: ..., CleanupInterval: ...})`) and no size/entry bound is evident in the diff, so sustained requests with varying names/folders can create unbounded numbers of denial entries for `shortCacheTTL`, creating memory pressure/DoS risk.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] userPermDenialCacheKey omits identity type and uses raw checkReq.UserUID, while the allow path (getCachedIdentityPermissions) caches under the resolved store.UserIdentifiers.UID — the two caches use divergent identity key spaces for the same decision. Denial entries are shared across identity types whose UserUID strings collide: identities that carry an empty UserUID (anonymous, and render-service checks) all land in the same key space for a given namespace/action/name/parent, so a denial incurred by one identity denies the other until TTL. The mismatch also means any future change to how GetUserIdentifiers resolves or normalizes UIDs silently decouples the denial cache from the allow cache, and the next maintainer adding an invalidation or a new identity type must remember to update two different key derivations for one logical concept.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows two different cache key derivations for related permission decisions: the new denial cache key is built from `checkReq.UserUID` without including `IdentityType` (`permDenialKey := userPermDenialCacheKey(..., checkReq.UserUID, ...)`), while the allow/permission cache for users/service accounts is keyed off the resolved `store.UserIdentifiers.UID` inside `getCachedIdentityPermissions` (via `GetUserIdentifiers` then `userPermCacheKey(ns.Value, userIdentifiers.UID, action)`). This is a real inconsistency introduced by the change and could become problematic if `checkReq.UserUID` differs from the resolved UID or if identity types can share/collide on the same `UserUID` string, but the diff alone doesn’t prove those collisions/empties occur in practice.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] permissionCacheUsage telemetry no longer measures permission-cache usage: denial-cache hits are counted as hits of the permission cache, and permission-cache hits whose evaluation denies are counted as misses before falling through to the database. On a permDenialCache hit (line 117-120) the metric increments with label "true" even though permCache was never consulted; on a permCache hit where checkPermission denies (line 133), it increments "false" and the request pays a full DB read even though the cache was hit. Operators tuning shortCacheTTL or evaluating this feature's hit rate from the permissionCacheUsage series will read a number that mixes three distinct behaviors (denial-cache short-circuit, permission-cache allow, permission-cache miss/deny), making the cache appear more effective than it is and hiding the DB-load cost of the deny fall-through path.

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, a `permDenialCache` hit short-circuits and increments `permissionCacheUsage` with label "true" (lines around the new denial-cache check) even though `permCache` was never consulted. Separately, when `getCachedIdentityPermissions` returns cached perms (cache hit) but `checkPermission` returns `allowed == false`, the code falls through, increments `permissionCacheUsage` with "false", and performs `getIdentityPermissions` (DB read), so the metric records a miss even though a permission-cache hit occurred. This makes the `permissionCacheUsage` series mix denial-cache short-circuits, permission-cache allow hits, and cache-hit-but-deny fall-throughs, reducing its usefulness for operators, but it doesn’t break authorization correctness.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" subtest cannot fail if the permDenialCache short-circuit in Check is deleted, because its cached-permission fixture is set to deny (map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}) even though its comment states the intent is to cache an ALLOW that the denial entry must override, and the request sets the Folder field while the lookup key is built from checkReq.ParentFolder so the pre-seeded denial key (with parent "fold1") likely never matches. The only test claiming to verify the new denial-cache short-circuit actually passes via the ordinary cached-deny fall-through-to-DB path (which also returns Allowed=false); a regression that removes or reorders the permDenialCache.Get check in service.go leaves this test green, giving false confidence that the feature this PR introduces is covered.
matched_golden_ids: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate highlights that the test comment/intent claims the cache contains an ALLOW, but the seeded cached-permission map actually stores `false` for `dashboards:uid:dash1`, so the permission check treats it as denied. This is the same mismatch described in the golden comment (even though the candidate adds extra observations about key mismatch/coverage).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] No test in this diff drives the permDenialCache.Set write path: every TestService_CacheCheck subtest pre-seeds the caches directly, and none runs a Check that produces a DB-backed denial and then asserts the denial was cached and served on a follow-up Check. The denial-cache round-trip (deny in DB -> Set on line ~153 of service.go -> subsequent Check short-circuits) is never verified end-to-end; a regression that stops populating the cache (wrong key, Set error swallowed, condition inverted) leaves the denial-cache fast path permanently dead while every test in the diff still passes. Test files checked: pkg/services/authz/rbac/service_test.go (the only test file touched by this diff; no other spec references permDenialCache or userPermDenialCacheKey).

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new denial-cache write in Service.Check: after the DB-backed permission evaluation, if `!allowed` it executes `s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)` (service.go around the added block after `allowed` is computed). The added/modified tests in `service_test.go` only (a) pre-seed `permDenialCache` directly (`s.permDenialCache.Set(...)`) to test the short-circuit deny path, or (b) exercise cached-allow and cache-miss DB-allow behavior. No test performs an end-to-end sequence where a first `Check` is denied via the DB path, then asserts that a subsequent `Check` is denied via the `permDenialCache.Get` fast path (and thus that the `Set` path used the correct key/condition). So the finding correctly identifies a specific, diff-grounded missing test for newly introduced nontrivial logic, not a proven functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new getCachedIdentityPermissions is only exercised for TypeUser by the new tests; its TypeRenderService branch (hard-coded ErrNotFound forcing a store hit on every render check), its TypeAnonymous permCache read, and its default unsupported-identity-type error return have no test coverage introduced in this diff. The deliberate render-service always-miss decision and the anonymous cache-read relocation out of getAnonymousPermissions are behavior changes nobody pins, so a future edit that silently changes them (e.g., caching render-service perms, or dropping the anonymous branch) ships without a failing test; additionally the default-branch error is unobservable through Check/List because both callers swallow any getCachedIdentityPermissions error into the DB fallback, making that branch dead code as wired. Test files checked: pkg/services/authz/rbac/service_test.go only; no test in the diff references TypeAnonymous, TypeRenderService, or getCachedIdentityPermissions error paths.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `getCachedIdentityPermissions` with distinct behavior for `TypeAnonymous` (reads `permCache`), `TypeRenderService` (always returns `cache.ErrNotFound`), and a `default` branch returning `fmt.Errorf("unsupported identity type")`. The newly added tests (`TestService_CacheCheck`, `TestService_CacheList`) only exercise the `TypeUser`/`TypeServiceAccount` path via `Subject: "user:test-uid"`; there are no new tests covering the anonymous or render-service branches, nor any error-path assertions. Also, both `Check` and `List` treat any non-nil error from `getCachedIdentityPermissions` as a cache miss and fall back to `getIdentityPermissions`, so the `default`-branch error from the cache function is not observable as wired, making that branch effectively unpinned by tests. This is a concrete, diff-grounded test/behavior-coverage concern rather than a proven functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The "List based on cached permissions" subtest relies on s.store being nil (so a cache-miss fallback would panic) to prove the cache path was taken, instead of asserting store non-invocation or the permissionCacheUsage metric. The test's cache-path guarantee is incidental: if setupService later gains a default fake store (or the fallback stops dereferencing it), the subtest keeps passing while actually exercising the DB path, silently losing its reason to exist; there is also no cache-miss subtest for the new List caching branch in this diff.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new caching branch in `Service.List` (it first calls `getCachedIdentityPermissions`, then falls back to `getIdentityPermissions` on `ErrNotFound`). The new test `TestService_CacheList` only covers the cache-hit scenario and does not include a cache-miss/fallback subtest for this new branch. Also, the cache-hit subtest asserts only the returned items/folders and does not explicitly assert that the cache path was taken (e.g., by verifying `permissionStore`/`store` non-invocation or checking the `permissionCacheUsage` metric). The specific claim that it "relies on s.store being nil" is not fully verifiable from the shown diff because `setupService()` is truncated and we can't confirm whether `s.store` is nil by default, but the broader point about the test not guaranteeing the cache path and lacking a miss test is diff-grounded.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The new permDenialCache entries written on every denied Check are never invalidated by any code path in the permission-change invalidation flow, unlike permCache entries which existing permission-update invalidation clears via userPermCacheKey-shaped keys. When an operator grants a user access to a resource (role change, dashboard share, team membership change), the invalidation that previously made the grant take effect immediately clears permCache but leaves the denial entry at 'namespace.perm_<uid>_<action>_<name>_<parent>' in place for the full shortCacheTTL — and the denial check at service.go:118-121 runs FIRST and explicitly overrides a cached Allow (the test 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' proves denial wins over an allow entry). The user continues to be denied access they now have, and the stale denial survives exactly the invalidation mechanism that made the pre-existing shortCacheTTL staleness acceptable.

adjudication.rationale: The diff clearly introduces a new `permDenialCache` (service.go: Check) that is consulted first and immediately returns `Allowed: false` on a cache hit, overriding any later allow outcome; the added test “Should deny on explicit cache deny entry” confirms this precedence. However, the finding’s central claim—that permission-change invalidation clears `permCache` but does not clear the new denial keys—is not verifiable from this diff because no invalidation flow/code is shown or modified here. What is verifiable is that a new cache key shape (`userPermDenialCacheKey(...)`) and cache (`permDenialCache`) were added without any corresponding invalidation logic visible in the patch, which is an important integration/edge-case concern but not a conclusively proven bug from the provided diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The PR's stated goal is moving caching from the client into the service, but newRemoteRBACClient still wraps the client in cache.NewLocalCache (30s expiry), so remote-authz-server deployments now stack a 30s client-side cache on top of the new service-level permCache/permDenialCache, while the in-process path (rbac.go:101-104) was switched to NoopCache. On remote deployments a permission change is now delayed by shortCacheTTL plus the 30s client cache (the inner service cache invalidates, then the outer client LocalCache keeps serving the stale Check response), and revocations — the security-sensitive direction — are affected; meanwhile the same code path behaves differently in-process vs remote, so cache-invalidation bugs will be untestable against the remote configuration.

adjudication.rationale: The diff clearly shows an inconsistency: the in-process client path in ProvideAuthZClient now constructs authzlib.NewClient with a NoopCache (rbac.go ~98-106), while newRemoteRBACClient still constructs authzlib.NewClient with cache.NewLocalCache(Expiry: 30s) (rbac.go ~157-166). This means remote deployments will still have a client-side cache layer whereas in-process won’t. The finding’s downstream impact (stale Check responses / delayed revocations) is plausible but cannot be conclusively verified from this diff alone because it depends on what authzlib’s client cache actually caches and how it keys/invalidates entries.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getCachedIdentityPermissions calls s.GetUserIdentifiers on every Check/List before probing permCache, and on a cache miss the subsequent getIdentityPermissions → getUserPermissions path calls GetUserIdentifiers again, doubling the identifier resolution per missed request. Every cache-missed Check (the common case for cold caches and for all denied checks, which always fall through to the full path per the 'outdated cache' flow) performs two identifier lookups instead of one, adding a redundant store/DB round trip on the hottest authz path; the change also silently increases load on idCache since the miss-side lookup runs even when the caller will discard the result on a permCache miss.

adjudication.rationale: Verified in the diff: `getCachedIdentityPermissions` calls `s.GetUserIdentifiers(ctx, ns, userID)` for `types.TypeUser`/`types.TypeServiceAccount` before probing `s.permCache` (new function in `service.go`). On a permCache miss it returns `cache.ErrNotFound`, and `Check`/`List` then fall back to `getIdentityPermissions(...)`, which (via `getUserPermissions`) calls `s.GetUserIdentifiers(ctx, ns, userID)` again (see `getUserPermissions` still starts by resolving identifiers). This creates redundant identifier resolution work on cache-miss paths (at least two id lookups / potential store hits), which is a concrete performance/load concern on a hot path but not a functional correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] permDenialCache entries are never deleted anywhere in this diff, and their key format (userPermDenialCacheKey) differs from userPermCacheKey, so any existing permission-change invalidation that targets the existing cache keys cannot clear them — while the denial-cache hit at the top of Check short-circuits before the DB fallback that was explicitly built to recover from stale denials. When an admin grants a user access to a resource (or changes their role/team membership, which invalidates permCache/idCache), a previously cached denial for that (user, action, name, folder) tuple keeps short-circuiting Check with Allowed=false until shortCacheTTL expires — the fall-through-to-DB-on-stale-deny behavior the diff itself adds tests for ('Fallback to the database on outdated cache') is defeated the first time a denial is cached, so permission grants stop taking effect on invalidation and only after TTL. The new test 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' also confirms denials override even a fresh cached allow, since the denial cache is consulted before permCache.

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the new `permDenialCache` is consulted first and immediately returns `Allowed: false` on a hit (`if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { ... return &authzv1.CheckResponse{Allowed: false}, nil }`). Later, when the DB-backed check determines `!allowed`, the code sets this denial entry (`s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)`). The diff shows no corresponding deletion/invalidation path for `permDenialCache`, and its key (`userPermDenialCacheKey(namespace,userUID,action,name,parent)`) is distinct from the existing `permCache` key (`userPermCacheKey(namespace,uid,action)`). Therefore, once a denial is cached, it will short-circuit before the “fallback to DB” logic and can remain in effect until `shortCacheTTL` expires, even if underlying permissions are subsequently granted, which is a correctness regression introduced by this change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The shared newRBACClient helper was deleted rather than parameterized by cache option, leaving two independent authzlib.NewClient construction sites (in-process with &NoopCache{} here, remote with cache.NewLocalCache at lines ~160-166) that must be kept in sync by hand. The next tracer/client option added to one construction site silently diverges the other — e.g., a tracing or dial option added only to the remote client leaves the in-process client (which serves every check when Zanzana shadow mode is off) without it, and nothing in the code flags the drift.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows two separate authzlib.NewClient construction sites: in ProvideAuthZClient it is built inline with authzlib.WithCacheClientOption(&NoopCache{}) and tracer (rbac.go ~98-106), while in newRemoteRBACClient it is built inline with a real local cache and tracer (rbac.go ~157-166). The prior shared helper newRBACClient(conn, tracer) that centralized these options was removed, so future option additions/changes could be applied to one client but not the other without any compile-time signal. This is a maintainability/consistency risk rather than an immediate functional defect proven by the diff.
